title: Integrals Involving Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
lead: The exponential function eˣ is its own integral, and x⁻¹ integrates to the natural logarithm of an absolute value. With substitution, these formulas integrate the models of growth and decay: a price–demand function recovered from its marginal rate, a bacteria culture, a population of fruit flies.
summary_html:
• Exponential and logarithmic functions arise in many real-world applications, especially those involving growth and decay.
  • Substitution is often used to evaluate integrals involving exponential functions or logarithms.

exercises.prompt: Find the antiderivative of the function using substitution: $x^{2}e^{-2x^{3}}.$

From Example 5.42, suppose the bacteria grow at a rate of $\kq(t)=2^{t}.$ Assume the culture still starts with 10,000 bacteria. Find $\kQ(t).$ How many bacteria are in the dish after 3 hours?

answer.solution: $\kQ(t)=\frac{2^{t}}{\ln2}+8.557.$ There are 20,099 bacteria in the dish after 3 hours.

[T] $y=\frac{x+1}{x^{2}+2x+6}$ over $[0,1]$

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, does the right-endpoint approximation overestimate or underestimate the exact area? Calculate the right endpoint estimate R50 and solve for the exact area.

[T] $y=-2^{-x}$ over $[0,1]$

answer.solution: Exact solution: $-\frac{1}{\ln(4)},R_{50}=-0.7164.$ Since $\kf$ is negative and increasing on the interval, the right-endpoint estimate overestimates the value of the integral, but it underestimates the area of the region (absolute value of the integral).

Compute the integral of $\kf(x)=xe^{-x^{2}}$ and find the smallest value of N such that the area under the graph $\kf(x)=xe^{-x^{2}}$ between $x=N$ and $x=N+1$ is, at most, 0.01.

answer.solution: $\int_{N}^{N+1}xe^{-x^{2}}dx=\frac{1}{2}(e^{-N^{2}}-e^{-{(N+1)}^{2}}).$ The quantity is less than 0.01 when $N=2.$

exercises.prompt: Show that $\int_{a}^{b}\frac{dt}{t}=\int_{1/b}^{1/a}\frac{dt}{t}$ when $0\lt a\le b.$
Use the previous exercise to find the antiderivative of $h(x)=x^{x}(1+\ln x)$ and evaluate $\int_{2}^{3}x^{x}(1+\ln x)dx.$
Show that if $c\gt 0,$ then the integral of $1/x$ from ac to bc $(0\lt a\lt b)$ is the same as the integral of $1/x$ from a to b.

answer.solution: Let $u=\frac{t}{c},$ so $du=\frac{dt}{c}$ and $\frac{dt}{t}=\frac{du}{u}.$ When $t=ac,$ $u=a,$ and when $t=bc,$ $u=b.$ Then $\int_{ac}^{bc}\frac{dt}{t}=\int_{a}^{b}\frac{du}{u}.$

exercises.prompt:
The following exercises are intended to derive the fundamental properties of the natural log starting from the definition $\ln(x)=\int_{1}^{x}\frac{dt}{t},$ using properties of the definite integral and making no further assumptions.

Use the identity $\ln(x)=\int_{1}^{x}\frac{dt}{t}$ to derive the identity $\ln(\frac{1}{x})=-\ln x.$

answer.solution: We may assume that $x\gt 1,\text{so}\;\frac{1}{x}\lt 1.$ Then, $\int_{1}^{1/x}\frac{dt}{t}.$ Now make the substitution $u=\frac{1}{t},$ so $du=-\frac{dt}{t^{2}}$ and $\frac{du}{u}=-\frac{dt}{t},$ and change endpoints: $\int_{1}^{1/x}\frac{dt}{t}=-\int_{1}^{x}\frac{du}{u}=-\ln x.$

exercises.prompt:
The following exercises are intended to derive the fundamental properties of the natural log starting from the definition $\ln(x)=\int_{1}^{x}\frac{dt}{t},$ using properties of the definite integral and making no further assumptions.

Use a change of variable in the integral $\int_{1}^{xy}\frac{1}{t}dt$ to show that $\ln xy=\ln x+\ln y\;\text{for}\;x,y\gt 0.$

answer.solution: Split the interval at $x:$ $\int_{1}^{xy}\frac{dt}{t}=\int_{1}^{x}\frac{dt}{t}+\int_{x}^{xy}\frac{dt}{t}.$ In the second integral let $u=\frac{t}{x},$ so $du=\frac{dt}{x}$ and $\frac{dt}{t}=\frac{du}{u};$ when $t=x,$ $u=1,$ and when $t=xy,$ $u=y.$ It becomes $\int_{1}^{y}\frac{du}{u}=\ln y,$ so $\ln xy=\ln x+\ln y.$

exercises.prompt:
The following exercises are intended to derive the fundamental properties of the natural log starting from the definition $\ln(x)=\int_{1}^{x}\frac{dt}{t},$ using properties of the definite integral and making no further assumptions.

Use the identity $\ln x=\int_{1}^{x}\frac{dt}{t}$ to show that $\ln(x)$ is an increasing function of x on $[0,\infty),$ and use the previous exercises to show that the range of $\ln(x)$ is $(-\infty,\infty).$ Without any further assumptions, conclude that $\ln(x)$ has an inverse function defined on $(-\infty,\infty).$

answer.solution: For $x\gt 0,$ the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 1, gives $\frac{d}{dx}\ln x=\frac{1}{x}\gt 0,$ so $\ln x$ is increasing where it is defined, on $(0,\infty).$ By the preceding exercise, $\ln(2^{n})=n\ln 2,$ which grows without bound as $n$ grows, since $\ln 2=\int_{1}^{2}\frac{dt}{t}\gt 0;$ by Exercise 383, $\ln(2^{-n})=-n\ln 2,$ which decreases without bound. Since $\ln x$ is continuous and takes values that large and that small, the Intermediate Value Theorem makes its range $(-\infty,\infty).$ An increasing function is one-to-one, so $\ln x$ has an inverse function, defined on its range, $(-\infty,\infty).$

exercises.prompt:
The following exercises are intended to derive the fundamental properties of the natural log starting from the definition $\ln(x)=\int_{1}^{x}\frac{dt}{t},$ using properties of the definite integral and making no further assumptions.

Pretend, for the moment, that we do not know that $e^{x}$ is the inverse function of $\ln(x),$ but keep in mind that $\ln(x)$ has an inverse function defined on $(-\infty,\infty).$ Call it E. Use the identity $\ln xy=\ln x+\ln y$ to deduce that $E(a+b)=E(a)E(b)$ for any real numbers a, b.

answer.solution: Let $x=E(a)$ and $y=E(b),$ so that $\ln x=a$ and $\ln y=b.$ Then $\ln(xy)=\ln x+\ln y=a+b,$ and applying $E,$ the inverse of $\ln,$ to both sides gives $xy=E(a+b),$ that is, $E(a+b)=E(a)E(b).$

exercises.prompt:
The following exercises are intended to derive the fundamental properties of the natural log starting from the definition $\ln(x)=\int_{1}^{x}\frac{dt}{t},$ using properties of the definite integral and making no further assumptions.

Pretend, for the moment, that we do not know that $e^{x}$ is the inverse function of $\ln x,$ but keep in mind that $\ln x$ has an inverse function defined on $(-\infty,\infty).$ Call it E. Show that $E'(t)=E(t).$

answer.solution: $x=E(\ln(x)).$ Then, $1=\frac{E'(\ln x)}{x}\;\text{or}\;x=E'(\ln x).$ Since any number t can be written $t=\ln x$ for some x, and for such t we have $x=E(t),$ it follows that for any $t,E'(t)=E(t).$

exercises.prompt: The sine integral, defined as $S(x)=\int_{0}^{x}\frac{\sin t}{t}dt$ is an important quantity in engineering. Although it does not have a simple closed formula, it is possible to estimate its behavior for large x. Show that for $k\ge1,|S(2\pi k)-S(2\pi(k+1))|\le\frac{1}{k(2k+1)\pi}.$ $(Hint\text{:}\;\sin(t+\pi)=-\sin t)$

answer.solution: $S(2\pi(k+1))-S(2\pi k)=\int_{2\pi k}^{2\pi k+\pi}\frac{\sin t}{t}dt+\int_{2\pi k+\pi}^{2\pi k+2\pi}\frac{\sin t}{t}dt.$ In the second integral let $t=s+\pi;$ by the hint $\sin t=-\sin s,$ and it becomes $-\int_{2\pi k}^{2\pi k+\pi}\frac{\sin s}{s+\pi}ds.$ So the difference is $\int_{2\pi k}^{2\pi k+\pi}\sin t\left(\frac{1}{t}-\frac{1}{t+\pi}\right)dt=\int_{2\pi k}^{2\pi k+\pi}\frac{\pi\sin t}{t(t+\pi)}dt.$ On this interval $\sin t\ge 0$ and $t(t+\pi)\ge 2\pi k(2\pi k+\pi)=2\pi^{2}k(2k+1),$ so the difference is nonnegative and, by the comparison theorem, at most $\frac{\pi}{2\pi^{2}k(2k+1)}\int_{2\pi k}^{2\pi k+\pi}\sin t\,dt=\frac{\pi\cdot 2}{2\pi^{2}k(2k+1)}=\frac{1}{k(2k+1)\pi}.$

exercises.prompt: [T] The normal distribution in probability is given by $p(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-{(x-\mu )}^{2}/2\sigma^{2}},$ where σ is the standard deviation and μ is the average. The standard normal distribution in probability, $p_{s},$ corresponds to $\mu =0\;\text{and}\;\sigma =1.$ Compute the right endpoint estimates $R_{10}\;\text{and}\;R_{100}$ of $\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2}}dx.$

answer.solution: $R_{10}=0.6811,R_{100}=0.6827$
